title: The Trolley Problem
sources: Philippa Foot, “The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect,” Oxford Review 5 (1967)
Judith Jarvis Thomson, “Killing, Letting Die, and the Trolley Problem,” The Monist 59 (1976); “The Trolley Problem,” Yale Law Journal 94 (1985)

segments.text: In 1967, the philosopher Philippa Foot imagined the driver of a runaway trolley.
Ahead, five people are working on the track. [[0.35]] On a side track, there is just one.
Foot thought the answer was clear. Whatever he does, the driver kills. [[quote 0.3]] So, “without hesitation,” he should steer for the less occupied track.
Then Judith Jarvis Thomson changed one detail. [[fainted 0.4]] The driver has fainted. [[you 0.3]] You are a bystander, standing next to a switch.
If you do nothing, the trolley will kill the five. [[pull 0.8]] If you pull the lever, it will turn onto the side track, and kill the one.

Most people say yes. But notice what changed. [[driver 0.5]] The driver chose between killing one, and killing five. [[you 0.5]] You choose between killing one, and letting five die. [[harm 0.5]] And doing harm usually seems worse than merely allowing it. [[why 0.7]] So why is pulling the lever permissible?
Thomson's first answer: [[0.3]] you don't create a new threat. You redirect one that already exists, [[move 0.2]] away from five people, toward one.

But in 2008, she changed her mind. [[third 0.4]] Imagine a third track, where you yourself are standing. [[few 0.4]] Few of us would turn the trolley onto ourselves. [[right 0.4]] And if you wouldn't, Thomson argued, you have no right to turn it onto a stranger. [[wallet 0.4]] That would be like stealing someone's wallet to give to charity.
So, would you pull the lever? And why?

This is the trolley problem in its simplest form. Philosophers have since built many harder variations, [[bridge]] like pushing a stranger off a footbridge to stop the trolley. [[point 0.6]] The scenario is deliberately artificial. [[0.3]] Strip a moral choice down to its bare bones, and it shows us what we really value.

publish.summary:
A runaway trolley is heading for five people. You can pull a lever to send it onto a side track, where it will kill one person instead. Should you?

Philippa Foot introduced the case in 1967, and Judith Jarvis Thomson turned it into one of the most famous puzzles in ethics: why does diverting the trolley feel permissible when so many other ways of killing one to save five do not? This short film walks through Foot's original driver case, Thomson's bystander version and the distinction between doing and allowing harm, and ends with Thomson's surprising change of mind in 2008.

discussion: Would you pull the lever? Leave your answer in the comments, along with your reasoning, especially if you can make the case for the other side.

Does your answer change if the only way to stop the trolley is to push someone off a footbridge? And is the trolley problem even a valuable thought experiment, or is it too artificial to tell us anything about real moral life?
Which thought experiment should we make next? Suggestions welcome.
